study.title: Acts 6 - Service in the church, growth of the Word and the beginning of opposition to Stephen
study.overview: Acts 6 shows an expanding church that needs to deal with internal tensions without losing its main mission. First, a legitimate complaint arises about the care of widows, and the apostles organize the community to preserve both practical justice and the centrality of prayer and the Word. Then the choice of seven men empowered by the Spirit paves the way for greater order in the service. Next, the chapter highlights the growth of the church and the performance of Stephen, whose wisdom, power and fidelity arouse opposition. The chapter ends with false accusations and the impressive scene of his face, which appears to the gifts with a glow similar to that of an angel.

outline.title: A real need in the community and the apostolic priority
outline.explanation: The growth of the disciples brings a complaint among the Greek-speaking believers and those of Hebrew speech, because the widows of that group were being neglected in the daily distribution. The apostles recognize the problem, but make it clear that it would not be right to abandon the Word of God to take on this task directly.

outline.title: Organization of service and dedication to prayer
outline.explanation: The church is oriented to choose seven men of good reputation, full of the Holy Spirit and wisdom, for this responsibility. Thus, the apostles continue to persevere in prayer and ministry of the Word, without despising the material care of the community.

outline.title: The choice of the seven and the advancement of the Word
outline.explanation: The proposal pleases all, and the seven are chosen and presented to the apostles, who pray and lay their hands on them. The result is the growth of the Word of God, multiplication of the disciples in Jerusalem and even the adherence of many priests to the faith.

outline.title: Stephen, the opposition and the countenance of an angel
outline.explanation: Stephen performs signs and miracles, but is now challenged by members of a synagogue. Since they cannot respond to their wisdom, his opponents resort to bribery, false accusations and public manipulation, leading him to the council. Even so, his countenance appears in the eyes of the present as that of an angel.

study.context: The text presents a conflict between groups of disciples identified as Greeks and Hebrews, showing differences of origin and custom within the Christian community in Jerusalem. The notes describe the Greeks as Greek-speaking Christian Jews, linked to the Greco-Roman world, and the Hebrews as more traditional Jews, native to Palestine. The chapter also places Stephen's action before Jewish leaders and a specific synagogue, culminating in his arrest and trial before the supreme council.
study.theology: The chapter teaches that the growth of the church does not eliminate internal problems; rather, it requires discernment, justice and good organization. There is a strong emphasis on the spiritual priority of the apostles: prayer and teaching of the Word should not be replaced by other needs, even though these are important. At the same time, care for widows shows that the Christian faith does not separate spiritual life from practical responsibility. The choice of men full of the Spirit for a daily service indicates that material tasks also belong to the field of life full of the Spirit. In Stephen, the text shows that fidelity, wisdom, and power in the Spirit can attract opposition, and that true testimony can be treated with false accusations. His angel's face suggests, on the narrative level, a divine approval and a sign of serenity before injustice. Some confessional readings see here a correspondence between Stephen and Moses, but this should be understood as an interpretation of the notes, not as an explicit statement of the verse.

scholarViews.insight: The apostles recognized the seriousness of the problem and the priority of the teaching of the Word, so the community chose wise and full men of the Spirit to oversee the distribution of food.
The church prudently resolved a domestic disagreement before it caused greater damage; the choice of the seven allowed the apostles to remain in the prayer and ministry of the Word.
The seven were assigned to oversee the temporal affairs of the church, and Stephen, full of faith and the Holy Spirit, is presented as one perfectly equipped for his function.

questions: How can the church treat legitimate conflicts without losing sight of its main mission of prayer and teaching of the Word?
What does it mean, in practice, to choose people full of the Spirit and wisdom for service responsibilities?
Why does Stephen's fidelity awaken so much opposition, and what does this teach about the cost of Christian witness?
study.practice: This chapter calls on the Christian community to unite spirituality and concrete responsibility. In practice, this means listening to complaints seriously, organizing service with justice, choosing trusted leaders and not abandoning prayer or biblical teaching. It also teaches that serving in seemingly simple tasks can be an important ministry before God. To today's believer, Stephen's attitude encourages to stay firm when the truth is attacked, without responding with violence or fear. A concrete application is to review how your church distributes care, leadership and prayer, seeking more transparency, more service and more dependence on the Holy Spirit.
study.uncertainty: The biblical text does not explicitly identify the exact meaning of the reference to the face as an angel's; the connection with Moses, mentioned in the notes, is interpretive. It is also not possible to state with historical certainty additional details about the synagogue of the freed beyond what the notes provide. Notes suggest that the seven can be seen as first deacons, but this is a comparative reading, not a direct statement of the chapter.
